passage: Diary. Manjula here, 9:40 pm. I heard Shreya's name in assembly again, this time for topping the mock test, and my whole body went hot. I didn't hear the rest of the announcement. All day I replayed things she has said, even things from last year. In maths I did four questions in an hour because I was busy being angry. At home I picked up my phone and started to type something mean about her to the class group, then stared at it for ages. I deleted it. Then I noticed something: I'd spent the whole day thinking about her, not about my own chapters. She isn't even here, and she's controlling my day. Tomorrow I'll make a plan for my own revision and keep her name out of it.

qa.q: When did Manjula write the diary entry?
Why did Manjula delete the message she started to type, and what did Manjula realise about the anger?
qa.a: Manjula chose not to hurt Shreya's reputation, and realised the hatred was tying up all that energy with Shreya so that Shreya was controlling Manjula's day.

qa.q: What would you advise Manjula to do next?
qa.a: Shift the focus to a personal revision plan and goals, as the diary plans, and if the anger stays strong, talk it through with someone trusted.

qa.q: How might Shreya see the situation?
qa.a: She may not know Manjula is angry at all, since the diary says Shreya isn't even there. She is probably just enjoying her result.

grounding: Manjula cannot bear hearing a rival's name, notices the hatred pulling attention toward Shreya, and turns to personal goals.

passage:
Dear Kamal Mama,

You asked on the phone why I sounded off. It's Uday. He got the lead speaker spot on the debate team, the one I've been working for since Class 9. Now I can't even hear his name without my jaw going tight. When Sir says "Uday, well done," I want to leave the room.

Last week I caught myself drafting a message to the team about how Uday's arguments were copied from videos. I have no proof. I just wanted people to think less of him. I didn't send it, but I thought about it for an hour.

Then I noticed something. I've spent more time thinking about Uday this month than about my own debating. Every evening goes into replaying his speeches and hating them.

So I've decided to stop giving him my evenings. I'm entering the inter-school elocution contest on my own, and I'll practise on you when I visit, if you'll listen.

Sahil

qa.q: What spot did Uday get on the debate team?
qa.a: Uday got the lead speaker spot on the debate team.

qa.q: What does Sahil's tight jaw at Uday's name suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Sahil feels strong resentment and hurt about losing the spot, enough that even hearing the name brings tension.
Not sending the message and entering the elocution contest worked, because it stopped an unfair attack and moved Sahil's energy to Sahil's own goals.

qa.q: How might Kamal Mama feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kamal Mama may feel concerned about how upset Sahil is, but also proud that Sahil did not send the message and chose a new goal.

grounding: It shows a teen consumed by hatred for a rival who notices that the hate ties up their energy and turns to their own goals instead of attacking the rival's reputation.

passage:
You want to know about the robotics olympiad thing? Fine. Anirban beat me by four points for first place in the regional round. Four. After that I honestly couldn't stand hearing his name. Whenever anyone mentioned him in the lab, I'd put my headphones on.

The worst part was I started planning. There was a clip of him tripping over a cable during the demo. I thought, if I post that with a stupid caption, everyone will laugh at him, and maybe the judges will see it too. I had the caption ready. My thumb was over the button.

Then my younger sister walked in and asked why I was grinning like that. And I realised I hadn't touched my own bot in two weeks. I'd been busy hating him.

I deleted the clip. Next day I rebuilt my bot's gripper. So that's me, Pranav, still annoyed, but at least working on my own thing again.

qa.q: How many points did Anirban beat Pranav by?
qa.a: Anirban beat Pranav by four points.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling while holding the clip with a caption ready?
qa.a: Pranav felt bitter and resentful, even a bit gleeful, wanting others to laugh at Anirban as payback for losing first place.

qa.q: What turned things around for Pranav, and what could keep it going?
qa.a: Noticing the bot had been untouched for two weeks turned things; keeping that focus on building the gripper and future rounds could keep Pranav going.

qa.q: What would have changed for Anirban if the clip had been posted?
qa.a: Anirban could have been mocked in public and his reputation hurt over a small slip, which would have been unfair and hard to undo.

grounding: It shows a teen who cannot stand hearing a rival's name, nearly plots to hurt the rival's reputation, then notices the hate draining their energy and refocuses on their own goals.
